chapter: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
title: Frank Walker's 1923 letter read into the tape
summary: Albertson reads Columbia's January 1923 letter asking about her Paramount contract and mentioning Joe Oliver's band as accompanists; they remark on the two-cent stamp, and she says no arrangements were used.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Of course.
Now, you want -- what else?
Yes. Do you want to stop just a second?
Did I put in -- yeah, you want to stop a little while, don't you, honey? All right. Yeah. Yeah, baby. Yes, darling.
We'll think about things to go into.
Yeah. Now, and that was -- that was -- what year was that?
We were just talking --
I know I married in -- you've got the year down, so you know what year that --
I wanted to read this letter you brought.
Help yourself.

Into the tape. It's from the Columbia Graphophone Company, 1819 Broadway, New York City, recording studios, dated January 19th, 1923, addressed to Miss Alberta Hunter, number 64 East 36th Place, Chicago, Illinois. "Dear Miss Hunter. Replying to your letter of the 15th instant, won't you please advise me at your earliest convenience just how long your exclusive contract with the Paramount Company runs. No doubt you know that the Paramount Company is very small indeed, and the prestige that you gain from singing for them is very limited. Regarding Joe Oliver's band, my only idea in this respect was to use them as an accompaniment for you in case you did work for us. It will therefore be necessary for us to forget them until such a time as you will be ready to do a test record for us. We will try to see what can be worked out of the "Downhearted Blues" for you. In the meantime I would ask that you let us know about the Paramount contract as soon as possible, so we can make our plans accordingly. With kind regards we remain very truly yours," and signed Frank B. Walker, Columbia Graphophone Company.
Now, you had apparently written them a letter about "Downhearted Blues".

He wrote me a letter first and I answered his letter. I don't remember what it was about, but he wrote me a letter first and I was answering his letter and in the meantime I mentioned something to him about "Downhearted Blues". That's how "Downhearted Blues" happened to be mentioned in his letter.
It's interesting. This is a letter going from New York to Chicago and it has a two cent stamp on it.
Isn't it interesting how times have changed.
(Laughter)
Isn't that something? Isn't that something? Two cents. That's right, from New York to Chicago. Now we pay 13 cents, don't we, now?
Yeah.
13 cents. And if you send a special delivery letter they don't send it special. They just send it along with the ordinary mail.
And in those days I think we had, up till recently, two deliveries a day.
Oh, absolutely. Absolutely.
So everything deteriorates.
Oh, everything, yeah. Now, Mr. --
So you never did record at that time
for Columbia.
At that particular time, no, not for Columbia.
And you apparently wanted Joe Oliver to accompany you?
Yeah. I wanted Joe Oliver to accompany me, because I was crazy about his work, and I knew if I had -- we didn't bother about arrangements at that time, you know.
Uh-huh.

Because if I started a song, you know, they'd just play what I -- you know, it looked like they would just feel what I wanted to do, you know, and just follow me along. We didn't bother with arrangements.
